title: Juzhi's finger
hookLine: a master raised one finger to every question; a boy copied him, and lost the finger (Gateless Gate 3)
last: BAIZHANG'S FOX — NOT BLIND TO CAUSE.

cards: A phrase that sounds wise can go around online in a week. The words spread, but the thing behind them doesn't always come along.
At work, the new hire copies the boss's way of talking, the pauses, the catchphrases, and somehow it doesn't land the same. Zen noticed this problem a long time ago.
Today's koan is the third in the Gateless Gate, and a warning up front: it's a shocking story. It's about a finger, and the difference between copying and knowing.

teach.b: A teacher named Juzhi had one answer. Whenever anyone asked him anything about Zen, he simply raised one finger. That was his whole teaching.
He had a young attendant, a boy.
One day a visitor asked the boy: what does your master teach? The boy raised one finger, just like Juzhi. When Juzhi heard, he took a knife and cut off the boy's finger.
The boy ran out screaming. Juzhi called his name. The boy turned his head.
Juzhi raised one finger. And the story says the boy was suddenly awakened. It's hard to hear, and it isn't offered as something to admire or copy.
Teachers who discuss it tend to call it a story told to shock, the way a parable exaggerates, and the Buddhist precepts begin with not harming living beings.

The Gateless Gate is a teaching collection, not a news report, and nobody knows what, if anything, happened. What the story points at is this. The boy's finger was a copy: the gesture without the seeing behind it.
Once the copy was gone, he had nothing to imitate when Juzhi raised his finger. He had to meet it directly, and something opened.

At the end of his life, the story goes, Juzhi said he'd received one-finger Zen from his own teacher, Tianlong, and used it his whole life without ever using it up. The finger was never the point. Seeing for yourself was.

how: Zen teachers use Juzhi's finger to warn against imitating a teacher's gestures or words; students are expected to respond to koans in their own way, not by repeating a known answer.

o: a raised finger meaning 'all is one' in Zen teaching
a hand sign Zen monks raise to ask for silence in the hall
a koan about copying a gesture versus seeing for yourself

games.q: a visitor asks you what your teacher teaches. you've watched her answer every question the same way for years. what does today's story point toward?
o: give an answer from your own seeing, even if it's clumsy.
games.why: the boy's copied finger was the problem; the story points to seeing for yourself rather than imitating.

practice: Think of one thing you say or do mostly because someone else does it, a phrase, a habit, an opinion you picked up; no judgment, everyone borrows. Ask: if I didn't have their words, how would I say this?
Let an answer come, or not, then rest your hands in your lap and feel your own fingers, warm and alive.

wordCard.voice: Juzhi's finger. A boy copied his teacher's one-finger answer, and only when the copy was gone did he see for himself.

orig.note: Chinese yī zhǐ: one finger, as in Juzhi's 'one-finger Zen'.

carryVoice: Your line: your own finger. A copied gesture isn't the same as seeing. Until tomorrow.
